To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) people with lower socioeconomic status and worse health are less satisfied with national healthcare systems than others; 2) people living in countries with higher power distance are less satisfied with their healthcare system than others; and 3) the relationship between power distance and health service satisfaction is mediated by people’s socioeconomic status.
people’s satisfaction with national health systems is influenced both by their own individual characteristics and by the national culture in which they live.
people who report poor health and unfulfilled health needs are less satisfied with their national health services.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between cultural values and the way people evaluate their national health systems.
the role of culture as a determinant of health system evaluation.
how cultural values influence citizens’ satisfaction with their national health system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

people in countries with a more autocratic and hierarchical national culture are less satisfied with their national healthcare system, and that this effect is independent of their individual characteristics and health status.
the more hierarchical a society is, the less likely its citizens are to be satisfied with their health system, even after accounting for the effects of individual level characteristics.
the higher the power distance, the lower the satisfaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more hierarchical the culture, the less likely people are to be satisfied with their national healthcare system.
people in cultures where power is more unequally distributed are less satisfied with their health services.
national cultures are likely to influence the way citizens evaluate their health services, and this effect is independent of individual socio-demographic characteristics and health-related factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cultural context in which a national health service operates matters for how citizens evaluate it.
cultural values are likely to influence citizens’ satisfaction with their healthcare systems.
national cultural values are important in understanding the public evaluation of healthcare services across Europe.
